entities.summary:
The First Opium War (1839-1842) was a pivotal conflict between the British Empire and the Qing dynasty of China, fought over control of the lucrative opium trade. This global event, which took place in the People's Republic of China, marked a significant turning point in Sino-British relations and had far-reaching consequences for both nations. The war began on March 18, 1839, when British forces, led by Admiral Charles Elliot, seized control of the port city of Canton (now Guangzhou) and ultimately led to the signing of the Treaty of Nanking on August 29, 1842, which ceded Hong Kong to the British and opened up China to further British influence. The war's legacy can be seen in the unequal treaties imposed on China, which contributed to the country's 'century of humiliation' and paved the way for future Western imperialism.

The war saw significant military and naval battles, including the Destruction of the Chinese war fleet at the Battle of Kowloon (1839) and the First Battle of Ningpo (1842). The conflict also highlighted the importance of British naval power and the role of the opium trade in British foreign policy. The war's outcome had a lasting impact on China's international relations, as it forced the country to open up to Western trade and influence, which in turn contributed to the fall of the Qing dynasty and the rise of modern China.

The war also had significant cultural and economic implications, as it introduced British culture and goods to China and created new opportunities for British merchants and traders. The war's legacy can also be seen in the ongoing struggles of the Chinese people for national sovereignty and self-determination.

As Lord Palmerston, the British Foreign Secretary at the time, noted, 'We have the power, and we have the will; we shall not be satisfied until China is opened to us, and we have a share in the trade and commerce of that great and ancient empire.'
